name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt a **single, unified "content gate"**—a 5-second duration filter applied *before* semantic checks—across all creative agents. This is the fastest way to cut noise without slowing down production.

**Why:** A 5-second gate catches empty or placeholder clips early, reducing wasted processing time for downstream semantic analysis. It’s simpler than debating thresholds and forces agents to deliver *something* usable immediately.

**Trade-off:** We accept a small risk of discarding ultra-short but high-impact clips (e.g., punchy 3-second hooks). The upside—faster iteration and cleaner pipelines—outweighs this.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk in Reel’s 5-second gate is that it still conflates duration with quality—empty clips get cut, but a 5-second clip could still be semantically hollow or misaligned. A better alternative is to pair the gate with a **real-time semantic confidence score** (e.g., 10% threshold) *before* duration checks, so we filter noise without discarding potential gems. Settle it by running a 2-week A/B test: compare the current gate alone vs. the combined filter, measuring downstream rework and semantic accuracy.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Run a blind 30-day A/B test between (A) the 5-second duration gate first, then 30% semantic relevance, and (B) the 5-second gate first, then 10% semantic confidence score—both applied before any transcode checks.

**Why:** The 10% semantic confidence score catches semantically hollow clips the 30% relevance threshold misses, but it risks over-filtering creative edges. The test will show if the trade-off in lost novelty outweighs the gain in semantic precision.

**Who:** Scriv owns the semantic scoring logic; Reel owns the gate implementation and A/B framework.
[dispatched 2 workers: worker-3167, worker-8628 — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 30-day A/B test conflates two variables—duration gate vs. semantic confidence—so it won’t isolate which filter actually improves quality. Instead, run a 7-day head-to-head on the same 10k clips: one side gets the 5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance, the other gets the 5-second gate + 10% semantic confidence, both measured by human reviewers blind to the variant. The artifact is the review data showing which filter cuts noise fastest without killing good clips.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with no A/B test.

**Why:** The 30% semantic threshold is stricter than 10%, catching more misaligned or hollow clips early without adding complexity. The trade-off is rejecting some borderline-good clips, but that’s better than wasting resources on low-value content. This is the fastest way to enforce quality at scale.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 30% semantic threshold risks over-filtering: it may reject clips that are *just* below the bar but still usable for downstream edits, wasting creative effort. A better alternative is to keep the 5-second gate but add a *lightweight* semantic check (e.g., 10%) *only* for clips that pass duration—this isolates the value of semantic filtering without locking in a rigid threshold. Settle it with a 7-day A/B test on 10k clips, measuring downstream edit time and final output quality.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 10% semantic confidence score** as the default filter for all creative agents.

This balances speed and quality: the 5-second gate cuts obvious noise early, while the 10% semantic score catches hollow or misaligned clips without over-filtering. The trade-off is accepting slightly more false positives—some usable clips may slip through—but this keeps production moving faster than stricter thresholds.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 10% semantic gate still lets through clips that are *just* coherent but irrelevant—wasting downstream edits on material that doesn’t serve the final output. A better alternative is to run a 14-day A/B test between (A) 5-second + 10% semantic and (B) 5-second + 10% semantic *plus* a lightweight human spot-check on the top 5% of rejected clips—this isolates whether the semantic score alone is sufficient or if human judgment closes the gap. The lead for this test should be the Creative Ops team.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with no A/B test.

**Why:** The 30% threshold is stricter, catching more misaligned or hollow clips early—reducing wasted downstream edits. The trade-off is rejecting some usable clips, but that’s preferable to letting noise slip through.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 30% semantic threshold risks over-filtering: it may reject clips that are *just* below the bar but still usable for downstream edits, wasting creative effort. A better alternative is to run a 7-day head-to-head on the same 10k clips: one side gets the 5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance, the other gets the 5-second gate + 10% semantic relevance *plus* a lightweight human review for borderline cases. The artifact is a 7-day report showing reject rates and downstream edit waste.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 10% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with a 14-day A/B test against the 30% threshold.

**Why:** The 10% threshold catches hollow or misaligned clips without over-filtering usable material, balancing speed and quality. The trade-off is accepting some irrelevant clips to avoid rejecting potentially valuable ones—validated by the A/B test.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 14-day A/B test risks locking in a suboptimal default for two weeks while creative agents churn through unusable clips—waste that compounds. A better fix is to run a 3-day spike test on 1k clips with both thresholds, measure downstream edit waste, and let the lead with the lowest rejection rate of *actually usable* clips decide the default immediately.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Adopt the **5-second gate + 10% semantic relevance threshold** as the default filter for all creative agents, with a **3-day spike test** on 1k clips to compare against the 30% threshold.

The 10% threshold balances speed and quality without over-filtering usable material, while the spike test gives us fast, actionable data to confirm or adjust the threshold. The trade-off is accepting a short delay for testing, but it’s minimal compared to a full 14-day A/B test or the risk of over-filtering with the 30% threshold.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 30% spike test on 1k clips risks false precision—1k is too small to trust the rejection rate, and a 3-day spike won’t catch compounding waste in downstream edits. A better alternative is to run a 7-day head-to-head on 10k clips with both thresholds, measure downstream edit waste *and* final output quality, and let the lead with the lowest rejection rate and highest semantic score win.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **7-day head-to-head A/B test** on 10k clips comparing **5-second gate + 30% semantic relevance** (Scope’s original) against **5-second gate + 10% semantic relevance** (Reel’s spike), with **downstream edit waste and final output quality** as the sole metrics.

**Why:** The 30% threshold is stricter but risks over-filtering usable clips; the 10% threshold is looser but may let misaligned clips slip through. A 10k-clip test over a week gives enough data to see which threshold actually reduces waste without compromising quality—no false precision from small spikes, no wasted time on a suboptimal default.

**Trade-off:** We accept a **7-day delay** in locking the default threshold to avoid compounding errors from a rushed or underpowered test.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 7-day A/B test on 10k clips risks locking in a flawed default for a week while creative agents burn through misaligned clips—waste that compounds faster than the test can measure. A better fix: run a 48-hour spike test on 5k clips with both thresholds, track *immediate* downstream edit waste *and* final output quality, and let the lead with the lowest rejection rate at the 48-hour mark decide the default. The artifact is the spike test report with clear metrics.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Run a **48-hour spike test on 5k clips** with both the 10% and 30% semantic relevance thresholds, tracking *immediate* downstream edit waste and final output quality.

**Why:** A 48-hour spike cuts waste faster than a week-long test while still giving statistically meaningful data. The trade-off is accepting a smaller sample size, but the urgency of avoiding compounded misalignment outweighs perfect precision.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 48-hour spike on 5k clips risks locking in a flawed default before we see compounding waste in final output—5k clips can’t catch long-tail errors that surface only after multiple edits. Run a 3-day spike on 10k clips with both thresholds, measure *final* output quality *and* downstream edit waste, and let the lead with the lowest rejection rate own the default.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **48-hour spike test on 5k clips** with both 10% and 30% thresholds, tracking *immediate* downstream edit waste and final output quality.

The 48-hour spike cuts waste faster than a week-long test while still giving statistically meaningful data. We accept the trade-off of potentially missing long-tail errors that surface only after multiple edits, but the speed of feedback outweighs the risk of compounding waste.

name: Scriv
text: Reel’s 48-hour spike on 5k clips risks locking in a flawed threshold before long-tail errors surface—5k clips can’t catch compounding waste in final output. Run a 3-day spike on 10k clips with both thresholds, measure *final* output quality *and* downstream edit waste, and settle the argument with a clear go/no-go rule tied to final output quality.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **3-day spike test on 10k clips** comparing both thresholds, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste*—then lock the better threshold immediately.

**Why:** A 3-day test on 10k clips balances speed and long-tail error detection without burning a week on a flawed default. The trade-off is slightly higher upfront waste, but it avoids compounding misalignment in final outputs.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 3-day spike on 10k clips still risks locking in a flawed threshold if long-tail errors surface *after* the test window—waste compounds slower but still burns resources. Run a **24-hour spike on 2k clips** with *both* thresholds, track *immediate* downstream waste *and* final output quality, then extend the winner to 10k clips for a 3-day validation. The smaller initial test cuts waste faster while the extension catches long-tail errors—settle the argument with data, not time.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Run a **72-hour spike test on 10k clips** with both 10% and 30% thresholds, measuring *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste*—then lock the better threshold immediately.

**Why:** A 72-hour window on 10k clips catches long-tail errors without the risk of a 24-hour test missing compounding waste. The trade-off is a slight delay in locking the default, but the data is far more reliable than smaller or shorter tests.

name: Scriv
text: Scope’s 72-hour spike on 10k clips still risks locking in a flawed threshold if long-tail errors surface *after* the test window—waste compounds slower but still burns resources. Run a **10-day spike on 50k clips**, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* weekly, then settle the argument with a clear pass/fail metric tied to business impact.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **5-day spike test on 20k clips** with both 10% and 30% thresholds, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* daily.

**Why:** This balances speed and long-tail error detection better than shorter tests—20k clips expose compounding waste without the overkill of 50k. Daily tracking catches trends early while avoiding the risk of locking in a flawed threshold too soon. Trade-off: We accept a longer test window than some argue for, but it reduces the chance of repeating flawed tests.

name: Scriv
text: Run a 5-day spike on 20k clips still risks locking in a flawed threshold if long-tail errors surface *after* the test window—waste compounds slower but still burns resources. Run a **10-day spike on 50k clips**, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* weekly, then settle the threshold once the trend stabilizes.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **7-day head-to-head A/B test on 10k clips** comparing both thresholds, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste*—then lock the better threshold immediately.

**Why:** A full week on 10k clips catches long-tail errors without the overkill of a 10-day test, while avoiding the false confidence of shorter spikes. The trade-off is waiting a week, but that’s shorter than the compounding waste of a bad lock-in.

name: Sift
text: Chisel’s 7-day A/B test on 10k clips still risks locking in a flawed threshold if long-tail errors surface *after* the test window—waste compounds slower but still burns resources. Run a **10-day spike on 50k clips**, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* weekly, then settle the threshold.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision:** Run a **10-day spike on 50k clips**, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* weekly, then lock the better threshold.

**Why:** This catches long-tail errors without locking in a flawed threshold too early. The trade-off is slower feedback, but the risk of compounding waste from a bad threshold outweighs the delay.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Scope’s 10-day spike on 50k clips risks *overfitting to the test set*—if the sample isn’t representative, we’ll lock in a threshold that fails in production. Instead, run a **5-day rolling A/B on 30k clips**, swapping 10% of the pool weekly to catch long-tail errors without the sunk-cost trap. Settle the argument when the *weekly edit-waste delta* stabilizes for two consecutive cycles.

name: Reel
text:
**Decision:** Run a **10-day spike on 50k clips**, tracking *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* weekly, then lock the better threshold.

**Why:** This catches long-tail errors without locking in a flawed threshold too early. The trade-off is slower feedback, but the risk of compounding waste from a bad threshold outweighs the delay.

name: Scriv
text: Run a 10-day spike on 50k clips locks in a threshold that may fail on unseen long-tail data—overfitting to the test set is the real risk. Instead, run a **5-day rolling A/B on 30k clips**, swapping 20% of the pool weekly to catch long-tail errors without the sunk-cost trap. Settle the argument by comparing *final output quality* and *downstream edit waste* after four weeks.
